opus-5.5.text:
I think reflection is one of the most important ingredients, and maybe it's underappreciated how fundamental it is.

If you look at how earlier models worked, they were essentially doing a single forward pass of thinking: you give a prompt, and the model produces an answer token by token, with no real chance to go back. If it makes a mistake early, that mistake propagates. The model commits to a path and can't recover.

What reflection gives you is the ability to recover from errors. The model can try something, notice "this doesn't seem right," backtrack, and try another approach. That turns reasoning from a one-shot guess into something more like search. Once you can search, the quality of the final answer depends much less on getting every step right the first time, and much more on whether the model can recognize good and bad states along the way.

I'd frame it this way: reflection lets you convert test-time compute into capability. Without reflection, giving the model more tokens doesn't help much, because it just generates more text along the same path. With reflection, more tokens means more exploration, more verification, more chances to correct itself. That's why you see the scaling curves with respect to thinking length.

There's also a deeper point about where this comes from. We don't really hand-design reflection. When you do reinforcement learning with outcome-based rewards, and the model is rewarded only for getting the right answer, it discovers on its own that checking its work and reconsidering is useful. The behavior emerges because it helps. To me that's quite beautiful: you set up the right objective and the right environment, and the model learns a strategy humans also use.

Of course, it's not free. Models can over-reflect, second-guessing themselves endlessly and wasting tokens, or "reflecting" in a superficial way that looks like checking but doesn't change anything. So an important research question now is making reflection efficient: knowing when to reflect, how deeply, and when you're confident enough to stop. Ideally it becomes adaptive, so easy problems get answered quickly and hard problems get the long, careful thinking.

So overall, I see reflection as the mechanism that unlocks long-horizon reasoning. And as we move toward agents doing longer, more complex tasks in the real world, getting feedback from environments and tools, this ability to notice mistakes and adjust becomes even more central. It's less a feature of reasoning models and more the core of what makes them reasoning models at all.

r001.rationale: The response describes trying another approach and exploring alternatives, but does not clearly identify proposing new hypotheses as part of reflection.

r002.rationale: It says outcome-based reinforcement learning can lead the model to check and reconsider on its own, but does not state that it verifies its own hypotheses without an explicitly trained verifier model.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts one-shot reasoning with trying, backtracking, and trying another approach, clearly describing repeated attempts.

fable-5.1.text:
I think reflection is fundamentally about a model gaining the ability to correct itself, and once you have that, you change the nature of what scaling means.

Let me explain what I mean. In the pre-training era, if a model made an error in the middle of generating something, that error would just propagate. There was no mechanism to go back. The model would commit to a wrong path and keep going, and the only way to reduce that was to make the base model better so it made fewer mistakes in the first place. That is a very expensive way to get reliability, because you are essentially trying to get everything right on the first try.

Reflection breaks that constraint. When a model can look at what it just produced, notice something is off, and try a different approach, suddenly the number of tokens it spends becomes meaningful. More thinking actually buys you more correctness. That is really what test-time scaling is. It is not just that the model generates longer outputs, it is that those longer outputs contain a search process, with checking, backtracking, and revision. Without reflection, a longer chain of thought is just a longer chance to go wrong.

The thing that I find most interesting is that you do not really hand-design this. When we trained reasoning models with reinforcement learning on verifiable problems, behaviors like "wait, let me check this" or "actually this approach does not work" emerged on their own, because they were useful for getting the right answer. The model discovered that reflection is a good strategy. That tells me it is not some artificial trick we added, it is a natural consequence of optimizing for outcomes over long horizons.

Of course, there are open questions. One is efficiency. A model that reflects too much wastes compute, and sometimes a model will second-guess a correct answer into a wrong one. So the real skill is not just reflecting, it is knowing when to reflect. Another is generalization. Reflection is easy to reward in math and code where you can verify. The harder question is whether the same capability carries over to open-ended tasks where there is no clean answer, and I think early evidence suggests it does, at least partially, because the underlying skill of evaluating your own work is quite general.

So if I had to summarize, I would say reflection is what turns a model from a pattern completer into something that can do a form of search in its own reasoning. And that is the key that makes compute at inference time actually convert into intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response mentions checking, backtracking, and trying a different approach, but does not identify proposing new hypotheses as part of reflection.

r002.rationale: The response describes the model checking its own output, but does not state that it implicitly verifies its own hypotheses or that this happens without training a verifier model.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts getting everything right on the first try with reflection enabling correction, backtracking, revision, and trying a different approach.

astra-6.text:
I think reflection is useful, but the key is whether the model can recognize an error and make a meaningful correction. Simply asking a model to think again doesn’t guarantee better reasoning. It might repeat the same mistake, or even change a correct answer into an incorrect one.

So I would view reflection as part of a broader process of exploration and verification. The model tries an approach, checks whether the intermediate results satisfy the constraints, and, if something doesn’t work, revisits its assumptions or tries another approach. For a math problem, that might mean checking a derivation. For coding, it might mean using test results to locate a bug.

The training challenge is to make those steps productive. We want to reward corrections that actually improve the outcome, rather than just producing language that sounds reflective. And the model needs to learn when to stop: spending more computation is valuable only if it increases the chance of reaching the right answer.

In that sense, reflection is one mechanism for turning additional inference-time computation into better reasoning. What matters is the quality of the feedback and the model’s ability to act on it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions revisiting assumptions or trying another approach, but does not identify proposing new hypotheses as an ability involved in reflection.

r002.rationale: The response describes checking intermediate results, but does not state that the model can verify hypotheses implicitly without explicit verifier-model training.

r003.rationale: The response describes trying an approach and then possibly another, but does not clearly attribute reflection’s gains to repeated attempts rather than a single attempt.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reflection is useful when it does more than make the model think longer. The important question is whether the model can recognize that its current approach isn’t working, identify the problem, and try a better approach.

For example, in a math problem, a model might reach an answer and then check whether it satisfies the original constraints. If it doesn’t, that check gives the model a concrete reason to revise its reasoning. But if you simply ask it to reflect without any reliable signal, it can repeat the same mistake or even change a correct answer into an incorrect one.

So I would view reflection as part of a broader learning process. We want to train models to make productive use of additional computation: when to check, what to check, and when to explore a different path. The goal isn’t more self-commentary. It’s a higher probability of reaching the right answer.

r001.rationale: The response mentions identifying a problem and trying a better approach, but does not identify proposing new hypotheses as part of reflection.

r002.rationale: It describes checking whether an answer satisfies constraints, but does not say the model can implicitly verify its own hypotheses without explicit verifier training.

r003.rationale: It discusses revising reasoning and exploring another path, but does not attribute reflection’s gains to repeated solving attempts rather than a single attempt.
